meta.title: Who really said "I would never want to belong to any club that would have someone like me for a member"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Woody Allen did say it, in Annie Hall (1977), but he introduced it as his paraphrase of Groucho Marx's club joke, which Quote Investigator traces to 1949.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I would never want to belong to any club that would have someone like me for a member'?
meta.ogDescription: Allen's Annie Hall wording, Groucho's joke: Allen says on screen that he is paraphrasing Groucho Marx, whose club-resignation gag dates to 1949.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: This exact wording is from Allen’s opening monologue in Annie Hall (1977), which he co-wrote with Marshall Brickman. On screen, Allen presents the line as his paraphrase of a joke “usually attributed to Groucho Marx.” The wording is Allen’s, but the joke belongs to Groucho.

source.heading: Where the line comes from

docMeta.dd: Woody Allen as Alvy Singer, in the opening monologue

source.excerpt: The other … important joke for me is one that’s usually attributed to Groucho Marx, but I think it appears originally in Freud’s Wit and Its Relation to the Unconscious. And it goes like this, I’m paraphrasing: Um, I would never wanna belong to any club that would have someone like me for a member. That’s the key joke of my adult life in terms of my relationships with women.
source.trailTitle: How the joke reached Annie Hall
trail: 1949: Quote Investigator’s earliest find of Groucho’s club-resignation joke is Erskine Johnson’s column in the Dunkirk Evening Observer (20 October 1949), tied to a resignation from the Friars Club. QI notes that the wording is “endlessly mutable” and that nobody has produced the actual letter or telegram (Quote Investigator ↗).

1951 and 1959: Groucho’s son Arthur Marx tells the story in Collier’s (13 October 1951). Groucho retells it himself in his memoir Groucho and Me (1959) (Wikiquote: Groucho Marx ↗), set at what Quote Investigator describes as a fictionalized club (Quote Investigator ↗).

1977: In Annie Hall, Woody Allen as Alvy Singer recasts the joke as “any club that would have someone like me for a member.” He credits it to Groucho, and also, wrongly, to Freud (Wikiquote: Annie Hall ↗).

The Freud claim: Film scholar Richard Raskin points out that “neither the joke itself nor any likely forerunner appears in that book.” He suggests that Allen was probably thinking of a joke in Theodor Reik’s Jewish Wit (Raskin, 16:9, 2007 ↗).
source.excerptNote: This is spoken dialogue, transcribed as on Wikiquote’s Annie Hall page ↗. The film says “wanna”, and the popular version tidies it to “want to.” Allen’s nod to Freud is the character talking, not a real source. The joke is not in Freud’s book (see below).

author.name: Woody Allen
author.heading: About Woody Allen
author.bio: Woody Allen is an American comedian, writer and director. He began as a gag writer and stand-up comic before making films. Annie Hall (1977), co-written with Marshall Brickman, opens with Allen as Alvy Singer speaking straight to the camera. In that opening he retells two old jokes, and the second is Groucho Marx’s gag about not wanting to join any club that would have him.

misattribution.heading: Whose joke is it?
misattribution.intro: This is an odd case. The popular credit to Woody Allen is accurate for the wording, because he really did say this sentence on film. But the joke isn’t his, and Allen says so himself in the same breath. A second credit, the one Allen gives to Freud, doesn’t hold up.

items.why: Allen introduces the line as a joke “usually attributed to Groucho Marx” and says “I’m paraphrasing” (Wikiquote: Annie Hall ↗). Groucho’s club-resignation gag was in print by 1949 in versions like “any club that would accept me as one of its members” (Quote Investigator ↗).

Alvy says the joke “appears originally in Freud’s Wit and Its Relation to the Unconscious.” Richard Raskin found that neither the joke nor any likely forerunner is in that book. He points to Theodor Reik’s Jewish Wit as the probable mix-up (Raskin, 16:9 ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The joke is Groucho Marx’s, traced to 1949. The sentence “I would never wanna belong to any club that would have someone like me for a member” is Woody Allen’s retelling in Annie Hall (1977) (Quote Investigator ↗; Wikiquote ↗).

context.heading: Why Allen borrowed it
lead: Groucho’s gag was about a social club. Allen turned it inward. In Annie Hall it becomes a self-diagnosis, a neurotic’s inability to want anyone who would want him back, and he calls it “the key joke of my adult life in terms of my relationships with women.”

Richard Raskin reads the joke in the film as a “self-diagnostic tool” for Alvy and for the audience (Raskin ↗). Because Allen’s version is so well known, his “someone like me” wording now often travels without Groucho’s name attached.
detailsBody: None of them can be settled. Quote Investigator notes that no one has presented the original letter or telegram. The reported wording varies from source to source (“would accept me,” “would have me,” “will accept me”), and so does the club. QI suggests using either Groucho’s memoir wording or the earliest 1949 version (Quote Investigator ↗).
context.pull: That’s the key joke of my adult life in terms of my relationships with women.
